title: Cloud/SaaS IQ/OQ/PQ — How Qualification Differs from On-Premise
summary: Cloud and SaaS platforms fundamentally change how IQ, OQ, and PQ are executed. The customer does not control infrastructure, cannot perform traditional installation verification, and must adapt qualification protocols to the shared-responsibility model.

iq_differences.traditional_on_premise: Verify hardware specs, OS version, database version, network config, disk space, software installation checksums, and environment configuration match the Design Specification.

cloud_saas_approach.what_changes: You do NOT install anything. The vendor manages infrastructure. Traditional IQ (verify server, verify OS, verify database) is replaced by VENDOR QUALIFICATION.
what_to_do: Obtain and review vendor's SOC 2 Type II report — covers infrastructure controls, availability, security
Obtain vendor's ISO 27001 certification — covers information security management
Review vendor's system status history — uptime, incident frequency, resolution times
Verify vendor's data center certifications (if applicable)
Document the vendor's SLA commitments: uptime guarantee, RTO, RPO, data sovereignty
Verify your org/tenant configuration matches your Configuration Specification — this is your 'installation'
Verify integrations are connected and authenticated
Verify data migration completed successfully (if applicable)
cloud_saas_approach.deliverable: Installation Qualification Report that documents vendor qualification evidence and tenant configuration verification

oq_differences.traditional_on_premise: Execute scripted test protocols for each function in the Functional Specification. Test in your controlled environment.

cloud_saas_approach.what_changes: The test environment is a sandbox/copy of the vendor's cloud platform. You do not control the underlying infrastructure. Test execution is the same (scripted OQ protocols), but you must account for vendor-managed components.
key_considerations: Test in a FULL-COPY sandbox that mirrors production configuration — developer sandboxes may not have sufficient parity
OQ scripts are REUSABLE across vendor releases — build a regression test suite from OQ scripts that can be re-executed quickly
Include integration testing — verify that data flows correctly between the cloud platform and connected systems
Test under both normal and stress conditions (see FDA guidance on dynamic testing)
Document any vendor-managed functions that you CANNOT test directly (e.g., encryption at rest, backup processes) — reference vendor certifications instead
cloud_saas_approach.deliverable: Operational Qualification Report with scripted test results, including any vendor-managed functions documented by reference

pq_differences.traditional_on_premise: Run the system under production conditions with real users and production-representative data to verify consistent performance.

cloud_saas_approach.what_changes: Performance and scalability are largely the vendor's responsibility. Your PQ focuses on YOUR data volumes, YOUR workflows, and YOUR user population.
key_considerations: Scalability is the vendor's problem — but YOUR data volumes and query complexity can still cause performance issues
Test with production-representative data volumes (not just 10 test records)
Test concurrent user scenarios relevant to your deployment (e.g., 50 field reps syncing at 8 AM)
Test mobile/offline scenarios if applicable (see val-faq-006)
Monitor performance during initial production use — first 30 days should include enhanced monitoring
Vendor SLA provides the performance baseline — your PQ verifies your specific workload performs within acceptable bounds
cloud_saas_approach.deliverable: Performance Qualification Report documenting production readiness with your specific data, users, and workflows

vendor_responsible: Encryption at rest and in transit
customer_responsible: User access management and periodic review

gotcha: Do NOT skip IQ just because 'it is cloud.' Replace traditional IQ with vendor qualification + tenant configuration verification. An inspector will ask how you verified the platform is suitable for GxP use — 'it is Salesforce' is not an acceptable answer.

title: Maintaining Validated State — Change Control for Cloud/SaaS Platforms
summary: Once a cloud system is validated, maintaining that validated state requires a structured change control process. Unlike on-premise systems where you control when updates are applied, cloud platforms push updates on the vendor's schedule.

four_step_change_control.description: Adapted from the Salesforce Part 11 whitepaper's recommended approach for maintaining a validated cloud system.

Step 1 — Release Assessment.when: When vendor announces an upcoming release (e.g., Salesforce Spring/Summer/Winter releases)
activities: Review release notes for changes to GxP-critical functionality
Classify each change: No Impact / Minor Impact / Major Impact on validated functions
Document the assessment in a Release Assessment Record
Determine testing scope: None / Regression / Partial Revalidation / Full Revalidation
Step 1 — Release Assessment.timeline: Complete assessment 2-4 weeks before release date. For Salesforce, use the sandbox preview period.

Step 2 — Sandbox Testing.when: When release preview is available in sandbox
activities: Execute regression test suite (built from OQ scripts) in sandbox
Test any functions flagged as impacted in Step 1
Document test results — quantified where possible (see FDA guidance)
Identify and document any deviations or unexpected behavior
Step 2 — Sandbox Testing.timeline: Complete testing before release hits production

Step 3 — Production Verification.when: Immediately after release is applied to production
activities: Execute a targeted smoke test of critical GxP functions in production
Verify audit trail functionality is intact
Verify electronic signature functionality (if applicable)
Verify integrations are functioning
Confirm user access and security controls are unchanged
Update Validation Summary Report addendum documenting the release assessment and testing
Update RTM if new functions were validated or existing coverage changed
File the Release Assessment Record in the validation documentation set
Close out any deviations with corrective actions

internal_change_control.description: Changes initiated by YOUR organization (not vendor releases) to the validated system
examples: Changes to user profiles or permission sets
New reports or dashboards used for GxP decisions
process: 1. Change Request — Document what is changing and why
2. Impact Assessment — Assess impact on validated functionality using RTM
3. Testing — Execute targeted testing of new/changed functionality plus regression of adjacent functions
4. Approval — QA review and approval before production deployment
5. Deployment — Deploy change to production following approved plan
7. Documentation — Update validation deliverables (URS, FS, RTM, VSR addendum)

gotcha: Salesforce releases are AUTO-DEPLOYED to production — you cannot prevent them. Your release assessment process must be PROACTIVE. If you learn about a breaking change after it hits production, you are in a deviation state and must execute corrective action.

title: Salesforce Part 11 Compliance — Cross-Reference
summary: For the detailed §11.10(a-k) compliance mapping between Part 11 requirements and Salesforce platform capabilities, see the dedicated file: salesforce-part11-mapping.json (entries val-sfdc-001 through val-sfdc-008+). That file covers every sub-section with platform capabilities, customer responsibilities, known gaps, and electronic signature controls (§11.50, §11.70, §11.100, §11.200, §11.300).
key_takeaway: Salesforce is NOT 'Part 11 compliant' out of the box. The platform provides capabilities that ENABLE compliance, but the customer must configure, validate, and maintain those capabilities.

title: SaaS Validation Lifecycle — Continuous Compliance Model
summary: Traditional validation follows a project-based model: validate once, then maintain. SaaS platforms require a CONTINUOUS compliance model because the vendor continuously updates the platform. This entry expands on val-meth-006 with operational details for sustaining validation in a SaaS environment.

Phase 1 — Initial Validation.description: Standard CSV/CSA validation of the initial implementation
Phase 1 — Initial Validation.activities: URS, FS, FRA, IQ (vendor qualification), OQ, PQ, RTM, VSR
Phase 1 — Initial Validation.outcome: System enters validated state. Baseline established.

Phase 2 — Vendor Release Management.description: Ongoing assessment of vendor-initiated changes (typically 3 releases per year for Salesforce)
activities: Release assessment per four-step process (see val-cloud-002)
Regression testing in sandbox
Production smoke testing
Documentation updates
Phase 2 — Vendor Release Management.frequency: Per vendor release cycle (every ~4 months for Salesforce)
Phase 2 — Vendor Release Management.key_metric: Time from release announcement to completed assessment — target < 2 weeks

Phase 3 — Internal Change Management.description: Managing changes initiated by your organization
activities: Change request and impact assessment
Testing of new/changed functionality
Regression testing of adjacent functions
QA approval and documentation
Phase 3 — Internal Change Management.frequency: As changes occur — can be sprint-aligned

Phase 4 — Periodic Review.description: Systematic review of the validated system to confirm ongoing compliance
activities: Review all changes since last periodic review (vendor + internal)
Review audit trail for anomalies
Review access control — deactivated accounts, role changes, periodic access recertification
Review incidents/deviations and their resolutions
Review vendor's latest SOC 2 / certification reports
Review training records — are all users current?
Verify backup/restore capability
Update risk assessment if system scope has changed
Phase 4 — Periodic Review.frequency: Annually (minimum). High-risk systems may warrant semi-annual review.
Phase 4 — Periodic Review.deliverable: Periodic Review Report documenting findings and corrective actions

activities: Monitor vendor's Trust/Status site for incidents affecting your instance
Monitor audit trail for unauthorized changes or unusual activity
Track and investigate user-reported issues
Monitor integration health
Track vendor security advisories

operational_kpis.Release Assessment Completion: 100% of vendor releases assessed before production deployment
operational_kpis.Regression Test Pass Rate: > 95% of regression tests pass on each release (failures require deviation)
operational_kpis.Change Control Compliance: 100% of changes go through formal change control
operational_kpis.Periodic Review On-Time: Periodic reviews completed within 30 days of scheduled date
operational_kpis.Training Currency: > 95% of users have current training records

gotcha: The biggest failure mode in SaaS validation is NOT the initial validation — it is the ongoing compliance. Organizations validate once, then fail to maintain the vendor release assessment process. After 2-3 missed release assessments, the system is effectively in an unvalidated state.
